speakerposition: stagedirection

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: PRESS REPORT AS TO JAPANESE FISHING FLEET OFF B.C. COAST
speechtext:
I
should like to ask the Minister of Fisheries a question connected with the Japanese fishing treaty. Is there any truth in the report by Mr. Elmore Philpott of the Vancouver Sun that Japanese fishing vessels are operating

Inquiries of the Ministry a hundred miles off the British Columbia coast and endangering the livelihood of British Columbia fishermen?

speakeroldname: Hon. R. W. Mayhew (Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
maintopic: PRESS REPORT AS TO JAPANESE FISHING FLEET OFF B.C. COAST
speechtext:
I have seen that article in the Vancouver Sun. This morning I took the trouble to inquire through our office in British Columbia, which, in turn, got in touch with the weather ships off the coast, with B.C. packers and with our own patrol boats, and I am now assured there are no Japanese fishermen within one hundred miles of our shore line in the Pacific.
While I am on my feet may I repeat a statement I have made frequently, not only in this house but in other places, that Japanese nationals have never fished along the British Columbia coast. At one time they fished in Bristol bay for a matter of two days. Conditions were made rather unpleasant for them, with the result that they left Bristol bay, came down the coast, got supplies in Seattle and went back to Japan. But they did not fish. The statement attributed to Mr. Philpott is therefore untrue. There are no such fishermen on the coast today, and there have not been, up to date.

On the order for committee of supply:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had a word with the leaders of the various parties and it was agreed unanimously that we should proceed in committee of supply and committee of ways and means to deal with the usual interim supply for the first two months of the coming fiscal year and then take up the final supplementary estimates.

Mr. Speaker, is my understanding correct that if you leave the chair it will be for the purpose not merely of dealing with interim supply but also of going into committee on the supplementary estimates? I wished to have a few words to say on the supplementary estimates and if this is the appropriate moment, I can say them now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Of course my hon. friend can make his remarks at any time, but he will realize that we will be going into and out of committee of supply several times before we get interim supply through, and before we get the items of the supplementary estimates voted and the appropriate supply bills based upon them put through. So far as I am concerned, I have no objection to his making his remarks at any time he sees fit.
Supply

I think perhaps I had better do it now, and then we may have the pain behind us. I want to say a word which I have no doubt has been said before, but which I hope will never have to be said again. I want to refer to the practice which seems to be growing of bringing down these supplementary estimates just far enough in advance of the end of the year to put the proper amount of pressure on the opposition to be good boys and carry them through. I am not arguing about bringing them down a day earlier; I am arguing about bringing them down a week or two earlier so that this important matter can be dealt with as it should be. I am going to suggest very earnestly that what has become almost a routine procedure could be abandoned in future with great profit to all of us.
Just a word about the size of the supplementary estimates. Two hundred and forty-six million dollars is a lot of money. One can cast his mind back not so many years ago when that would represent a large percentage of the total expenditures for the year. But when one examines this figure it is not so much its size that strikes one as the fact that there are one or two items included in it which almost seem to suggest that, for reasons which I do not understand, the minister wishes to inflate the figure as high as he can. It may be that the minister has a prudent eye on the political situation and is looking ahead, but there are two items here, one of $102 million and the other of $37 million-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Fifty-seven million.
For Polymer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: 1 beg your pardon; I thought you were referring to old age pensions.

The $57 million has to do with old age pensions, and that amount is in a different category. This item of $102 million would appear almost like an act of repentance and reparation. For a long time we appear to have neglected the superannuation fund of the civil service, but we are now trying to make up for lost ground and this year we have an item totalling $102 million. I think that compares with the $75 million a year ago. No one can question the propriety of that. Of course we have to have a sound fund. All I am pointing out is that there are people who are suggesting that this $102 million does not actually have to come in this year. They are suggesting that it and one or two other items are perhaps put in with a view to cutting down the minister's surplus, of which he spoke so proudly in the middle of February, but with a pride which perhaps is subject to qualification later on.

Supply
On that I have no view at all. I am just raising the point as it has been raised, and it is conceivable that this $102 million may-have come in wholly because the minister thought it was a matter of prudent bookkeeping to show what I suppose is a liability. We shall learn more about that later. But there is also the possibility that the minister thought it would be desirable to bring this in -he might as well be hanged for a sheep as a lamb-at this moment and get it behind him and be that much better off next year when possibly there may be reasons for trying to gentle the electorate.
The other item I wish to refer to is one dealing with Polymer. There I am even more surprised, because that item of $37 million is shown as part of this $246 million. If I understand the transaction correctly, it is what may euphemistically be called a bookkeeping transaction and does not actually represent an outlay of $37 million. I assume that when the budget comes out perhaps this-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not a budgetary item at all.

It is in here as part of the $246 million, if my addition is correct, and I tried to do my best to add it up. I think the minister will find that it is part of the $246 million, although the minister now says that it is not a budgetary item. I do point out it is included in the $246 million, and as such has gone out to the public as part of the supplementary estimates which we are now asked to vote.
I want to mention one further thing in passing. We have heard of the $722 million surplus. I do not know what we are going to be told is the final state of that, whether the final stage will be found to be larger than the first. It has been suggested it might be cut down a good deal. When the minister does explain it, if in fact it is reduced, I hope he will also explain what he said in February in his broadcast. As I read it in my simple way, it seemed to me he had explained that the $722 million had been very fortunate for the taxpayers of Canada, because, he said, it had made it possible for the federal government to do its national duty without invading the already tight capital market. In other words, if I understand the minister correctly, he indicated to us then that the moneys had been spent.
I should like to make one comment on the surplus. There are few of us who can arrange our own income to the extent the minister can. Perhaps that is a very comfortable position for the Minister of Finance, but it has its dangers too. What I mean is this, Mr. Speaker. After some reasonable representations to the contrary, last April the

minister did in fact add substantially to our taxes. I refer particularly to the sales and excise taxes. He did thereby add substantially to prices. In fact, if you take the whole effect of the year we had an increase in gross national product of $3,200 million, of which about $2 billion was represented by a rise in prices. To most of us that is very painful, except to those who are speculating and who are buying and selling on a rising market. It is not painful to the minister who gets a very large increase in his revenue. The Minister of Finance has been frank to point out to us that his increased revenues were, in fact, substantially due to higher prices.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext:
Order. Is the hon. member now discussing the problem of financing generally? I am afraid this will lead to a budgetary debate. I do not know what the arrangement was between the leaders of the parties as to my leaving the chair today without question put. Of course there is nothing before the chair at the present time.
I merely draw that to the attention of the hon. member, because I do not think he desires that we should have a general debate on financial matters at this time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact the Minister of Finance spoke to me, as I have no doubt he spoke to the leaders of the C.C.F. and Social Credit parties, I think I should say that there was no mention of the possibility of not having any discussion before Your Honour left the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is quite right, Mr. Speaker. Of course it is not necessary that a motion be put for Your Honour to leave the chair today. My understanding was that, by unanimous consent, we would proceed in committee of supply and ways and means to deal with the two items of interim supply and the supplementary estimates. I assumed that the discussion could range over any field that could properly be brought up under that head. I did indicate to the leaders the reasons why both supply bills had to be passed by both houses and receive royal assent before the end of the fiscal year. Aside from that, the hon. member is quite right, and the field is wide open for discussion.

Perhaps I could help by saying that I am just finishing my general remarks. I now wish to make one or two suggestions which I hope will aid the consideration of the items.
If I may just finish the comment I was making, it is this. Contrary to the rest of us, the minister gets tremendous boost from rising prices. I think we should remind ourselves, therefore, that it is not possible for the Minister of Finance, who after all is

naturally anxious to have a surplus, to have that detestation for inflation that the rest of us ordinary mortals have.
I want to make one or two brief suggestions about dealing with these estimates. I said that we object to their being brought down too late. I am afraid that we must face the fact that we have no feeling of sympathy with the government in trying to help them beyond a certain point. But on the other hand we have a great feeling of sympathy for anyone who is dependent upon getting these estimates through in order to get wages or salaries. We have, therefore, studied these estimates and have suggestions to make. We would distinguish between those which we think are of immediate urgency and those we think are not so urgent. While we are not foreclosing our rights to ask questions and discuss any of the items involved, in the case of those we think are urgent, for the reasons I have given, we are anxious to facilitate the passage of those items in so far as we can. We consider as urgent those items for producer assistance, wages or salaries or pensions of any kind.
If the minister will assure us that any item which I shall suggest is not urgent, in fact is for payments such as I have indicated, salaries or wages, we shall take his word for it and regard it as an urgent item. Actually I believe the minister will see that we have not gone out of our way to try to pick out items as not urgent. Most of them are indicated as urgent. I would just take a moment to indicate some of those that we think are urgent, and then indicate one or two examples of those which we think are not urgent. After that I suggest that we go through the items and when we come to one which we suggest to the minister is not urgent, we will ask him if he will allow it to go to the foot of the list and then he could make up his mind whether or not he agrees.
On page 1 of the supplementary estimates, item No. 563, which has to do with the foot-and-mouth disease, is urgent. We regard the subsidies to cold storage warehouses as urgent, and also the agricultural lime assistance. We have not done this in an arbitrary fashion. On the other hand, I could give one or two illustrations of cases which we think are not urgent. We cannot believe it is a matter of either twenty-four or forty-eight hour urgency that item 580 should be dealt with. It is concerned with commission for payment of interest. The payment of interest might be very urgent, but not this item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is to pay printing bills.
Interim Supply

Then, on page 5 of the supplementary estimates there are items dealing with certain indemnities for the Senate and the House of Commons. I am sure that all members will agree there is nothing urgent about that. I have taken it up with the authorities, and find that it does not affeot any member of the staff but only the members of the Senate and House of Commons. I feel sure that they would gladly go to the foot of the list.
I have tried to indicate that we are really co-operative, though we sometimes have to say somewhat critical things about the government; we always do it more in sorrow than in anger. We do want to co-operate, but with the reservation that we are not going to be panicked. As I say, co-operation does not involve acting in a mechanical manner. I hope the minister will agree with us when we come to those items we have marked as not urgent that we have tried to take a reasonable view regarding them.
The house in committee of supply, Mr. Dion in the chair.

Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Resolved, that a sum not exceeding $526,696,879.17, being one-sixth of the amount of each of the several items to be voted, as set forth in the main estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1953, laid before the House of Commons at the present session of parliament; and in addition thereto, a sum not exceeding $2,395,833.33, being five-twelfths of the amount of item 37, a sum not exceeding $526,420, being one-third of the amount of items 25, 448, a sum not exceeding $340,890.17, being one-sixth of the amount of items 209, 212, 213, and a sum not exceeding $257,602.41, being one-twelfth of items 62, 450, 452 of the said estimates be granted to Her Majesty on account of the fiscal year ending March 31, 1953.
He said: Mr. Chairman, the bill to be founded on this resolution is in the usual form. It will provide for one-sixth of all the items to be voted in the main estimates for the fiscal year 1952-53; an additional five-twelfths of one special item in respect of which charges will come for payment within, the first few months of the year, that is freight assistance on feed grain; an additional one-third of two special items for services coming for payment within the first few months of the year, those items being the compensation for animals slaughtered and items in connection with the international trade fair; an additional one-sixth of three special items which are to cover sessional expenses of the Senate and the House of Commons on which the heaviest payments fall due in the early months of the fiscal year; an additional one-twelfth of three special items which are for services of a

Interim Supply
seasonal nature covering citizenship and immigration, trade and commerce, electricity and gas inspection service and weights and measures division.
The general proportion of one-sixth, of course, as is usual is intended to provide for all necessary ordinary requirements of the public service to the end of May. The additional proportions requested for certain special items which I have indicated are necessary due to the seasonal and sessional services affected, and in no instance is the total amount of any item being released.
The form of the bill will be the same as the bill introduced at this time last year and for the previous year, except for the dropping of a section which authorized the raising of loans for the purpose of redeeming prior loans or obligations. That activity, commencing April 1, 1952, will be carried on under the authority of the new Financial Administration Act.
The passing of this bill will not prejudice the rights and privileges of members to criticize and discuss any item in the estimates which will come up for consideration from time to time during the remainder of the session. The usual undertaking is hereby given that such rights and privileges will be respected and will not be curtailed or restricted in any way as the result of the passing of this measure.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?
I wish to ask one question of the minister. There is usually an undertaking given in connection with this matter. At what stage will that be given?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have just given it.

I am sorry; I did not hear it. I thought I was listening, but apparently I was not. Will the minister comment on this point? The minister will perhaps remember that three years ago, when we were on the eve of an election, I raised with him the question of the undertaking which, as I recall it, was that these moneys are voted on the full understanding that parliament will have a chance to review the details. Is that the undertaking to which the minister refers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That has always been my understanding. This undertaking is in the form in which it has been given for some thirty years, I understand.

The minister will remember that there was a difference of opinion between us three years ago as to whether that meant that the undertaking was given to parliament, or to these members sitting in this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid that is beyond the power of this Minister of Finance or any other minister to say. .

Wait a minute; what 1 am referring to is this. There was a misunderstanding; I dislike misunderstandings, and I think it is time to clear it up. After all, the minister can construe the undertaking as well as any man in this house. I apologize for not having heard the words that he used.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will read them again.
If the minister would not mind doing so, he might perhaps read them again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
These are the words I have used every year since I have been minister, and they are the ones which my predecessor also used.
The passing of this bill will not prejudice the rights and privileges of members to criticize and discuss any item in the estimates which will come up for consideration from time to time during the remainder of the session. The usual undertaking is hereby given that such rights and privileges will be respected and will not be curtailed or restricted in any way as the result of the passing of this measure.
Does the minister not think it is perfectly clear that that is an undertaking to give to the men who sit in this house, who are the people who take this action-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Don't forget the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough).

I thank the hon. member for his assistance. I should have said, to the lady and the men who sit in this house. I think this is a matter of some importance, Mr. Chairman, because it became of importance three years ago. I should like to have the minister say whether, as I understand it, that wording means that that undertaking is given to those who now agree to take this action.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend wants my personal interpretation of what those words mean, I shall be happy to give it to him. It is an undertaking to the members of parliament, as such, who may be called upon to consider the estimates which I tabled a week or two ago, that the opportunity to discuss every one of the items in those estimates will be accorded to the members of parliament who are here, available and competent to discuss them. That is my personal interpretation. It may be right or wrong. In any event it is free. There is no charge for it.
It is worth the price.

The minister is not a lawyer for nothing. What I mean is that he has not wasted his time; but the minister has still not answered my question. He has worded his interpretation in such a way that it is open, I submit, to the construction that he is merely giving an undertaking that either the members who sit here now, or those who might succeed them after a general election, will have the opportunity to review these estimates. I was greatly surprised when that interpretation was given three years ago; and I suggest that if that undertaking means anything, it cannot mean that it is being given to a lot of people who are not here. After all, we are being asked to act. We are being asked to give this blank cheque which we give; but it has been on that undertaking. I confess until three years ago I had no doubt what that undertaking meant, but it was construed then in a way that I had not expected. I would greatly value the minister's opinion, which really he has not given. What I want to know plainly is this. Does the minister regard that undertaking as given to those of us who now vote in our individual capacity, or does he regard it as given to the abstraction of parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is an undertaking given to the House of Commons, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I say just a word in reply to one or two points made by the hon. member for Greenwood.
The method which is being followed as to the placing of these supplementary estimates before the house is the practice that has been followed for a great many years, under a great many administrations, both Liberal and Conservative. These are the estimates, which are substantial, to authorize the payment of bills. In only a few cases is there ever any question of any new policy being involved, and that is the case with these present estimates. They are, however, all items which relate to the fiscal year which is now ending. I shall be only too happy to co-operate with my hon. friends opposite in an orderly discussion of the estimates, and to give, or to make available, any information which may be necessary. But I must point out that the degree of urgency must rest with myself as the minister responsible for the placing of these estimates before the house.
The supply bill based on these estimates must be passed, as it invariably is, before the end of the fiscal year. If at any time some question arises about which the information is not readily available, and on which there may be an extended discussion, it might, as my hon. friend suggested, be useful to have it stand and deal with others on which there may be little or no discussion, and then come back to the other question and deal with it in a bit greater detail; but I must reiterate that these are all estimates which relate to the present fiscal year. The supply bill that will be passed will consist of one bill covering all of them.

I should like to make this comment, if I may, in answer to what the minister said. When I said that some were more urgent than others I was not suggesting that any were going to stand indefinitely. I only made the suggestion. The

only reason for our trying to make this distinction is that it might be more convenient, from the minister's own point of view, to take those that seemed, at any rate to us, to have that degree of urgency which I attempted to outline.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall be quite happy to cooperate in that. I think it is an excellent suggestion.

If we are dealing with item 563 I wonder whether the Minister of Agriculture is going to be in the house. I think he should be. However, in reply to what the Minister of Finance just said, item 563, which is before us now, is a very urgent matter. Yet to all intents and purposes the government has brought this item down on the last sitting day of the fiscal year-nekt Monday, of course, is private members' day.
I desire to take five minutes to discuss one particular aspect of this item, and I hope the minister will not tell me that the urgency is such that I cannot have that five minutes. This item is going to cost the taxpayers of Canada $665,000. I suppose it is the first instalment in the fight against foot-and-mouth disease. It is a very substantial sum of money, but I want to say that the amount is a fraction of what will be needed, unless we do something in the very near future to end these provincial embargoes against the movement of livestock. I understand that four provinces have a ban on at the present time. That embargo is having very serious effects.
In the first place, of course, it is completely disrupting the marketing of cattle, and is causing disastrous financial losses to many farmers.
In the second place it is creating a good deal of ill will and ill feeling between various provinces. For instance, I have an article in my hand which sums up the Alberta-British Columbia situation. This article was carried yesterday by the Canadian Press. It reads as follows:
Alberta, angered by British Columbia's reluctance to lift its embargo against Alberta meats and southern livestock, indicated yesterday it will seek a quick court test . . .
The article goes on:
At Victoria, Harry Bowman, British Columbia's agriculture minister, indicated that Alberta will have a fight on its hands. He said any challenge by the Alberta government will not bring any change in B.C. government policy.
The Alberta minister of agriculture went even further. A few days ago he threatened retaliation unless British Columbia lifts its ban. He said that Alberta may cut off the

export of oil into and through British Columbia. There are dangerous possibilities in the situation.
In the third place, these provincial embargoes are ill-advised, because they are giving examples to many foreign countries. Perhaps those countries may copy them.
This government should take immediate steps to test the constitutionality of these provincial bans. I think that Canadians everywhere, whether they are farmers, producers, consumers or packing house workers, want to know whether these embargoes are legal or not. I say that these restrictions which are today threatening to strangle interprovincial trade, are contrary to our constitution. I say further that the provincial governments that have imposed these embargoes are playing with fire, because restrictions of that kind can work both ways.
I think it is conceivable that if the provinces which have put on these embargoes persist with them, perhaps the governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta may be forced to consider retaliatory action. Perhaps they will be forced to consider whether it is advisable to put on counter-embargoes against such products as fish, lumber, fruit and certain manufactured goods. I admit at once that such a policy would be undesirable and most unfortunate. But I also say that the possibility does point out the dangers inherent in this present situation.
I was particularly surprised to read in the papers of the actions of the Quebec government in this regard. As long as I have been in politics I have heard Premier Duplessis scream from one end of his province to the other that the constitution is inviolate, and that under no circumstances should any of its clauses be disregarded. Yet he personally, without a second thought, tramples on the constitution, for the sake of political expediency. I think it is most regrettable, and I appeal to all the provinces to take some action to end this discrimination before the livestock industry of Canada, which after all amounts to more than $2 billion, is hurt for years to come.
I am not a lawyer, but as a layman it seems to me that the British North America Act says specifically that matters of trade come under federal jurisdiction. As far as agriculture is concerned, I believe that federal legislation likewise supersedes any provincial legislation that there may be. Why has the government been vacillating and so hesitant in getting a decision on this important matter? Last February 29 the hon. member for
Supply-Agriculture
Calgary East asked this question in the house, as reported at page 15 of Hansard:
Has the minister looked into or had determined the constitutionality of the action of some of the provinces in putting an embargo on all livestock...
And so on. The Minister of Agriculture replied:
Yes, the government has looked into it.
Then he said:
The general position is that in connection with agriculture and immigration, as is known in this house, both authorities have the right to legislate. But the general interpretation is that, where both have legislated, our legislation overrides the provincial legislation.
I think that statement was fairly definite. The federal government has whatever authority is required to take action in this situation; a month has gone by since the minister made his statement, but apparently nothing has been done. The embargoes remain. Yesterday I asked the Minister of Justice whether his department contemplated any action, and he made this answer, as reported at page 841 of Hansard:
As yet we have had no occasion to consider the legality of the bans.
Surely that was a most unfortunate answer. Here we have the livestock marketing industry of Canada slowly grinding to a halt and the federal Minister of Justice tells us that he has had no occasion to examine the legality of the bans. To me that seems very strange.
The opposite of what the Minister of Agriculture said.

Exactly. I am not going to take any further time, but I call upon the federal government to assume its responsibility in this regard, and to place some kind of an injunction with the courts, which will eliminate these embargoes without further delay. I think if the government refuses to take that action, even if the provinces later on agree to take it on by themselves, there will have been set a very serious precedent which, later on, could tear this country apart. That will be the condition if trade restrictions of this kind are going to be allowed. The farmers on the prairies today are looking to their federal government to protect them under the constitution.

I rise to a point of order, one which was discussed by the hon. member for Moose Jaw in the earlier part of his remarks. I refer to the absence of the Minister of Agriculture during this discussion concerning foot-and-mouth disease, and to the absence of other ministers whose departments will be affected as we go along. If the ministers are not going to be here I

suggest it becomes almost impossible to have any kind of reasonable discussion, or to have proper answers.
I do not expect that the Minister of Finance will be able to answer all the questions asked in connection with foot-and-mouth disease, or immigration, or many other matters. I suggest we should settle first, at this point, whether the minister should be here to answer the questions concerning his department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member, who has been in the house for some time, will understand that these are estimates to pay bills which follow as a result of policies already approved. The item before us now, for instance, is to provide the money to make possible what the House of Commons, after three days' debate a week or two ago, decided should be done. This item is to pay the bills only up to the end of the year. There is another item in the main estimates which we will be considering in due course and on which, I imagine, an extensive discussion will take place. There will be full discussion at that time, I should think, in respect of contagious diseases among animals,
I do not wish to hamper discussion in any way, but I must point out that if we duplicate debates four or five times, then it becomes difficult to provide for any sort of orderly discussion in the house. We have already approved the principle of paying compensation for these diseased animals. This is an amount sufficient to provide for payments that have become due by Monday night. There will have to be a further vote and, I am afraid, a very substantial one, to pay for what comes due after that time.
I will get such of my colleagues as are available but, as the committee will realize, there are other calls on their time, and it is difficult to have all of them in the house at the same time. However, I might be able to give the information in connection with this matter that the hon. member wishes to have, because all these items were carefully considered in treasury board in my presence.

Speaking again to the same point of order, and in reply to what the minister has said, while these estimates are for sums in addition to what we voted last year, I must point out that matters have changed considerably since we had our discussion at the beginning of the session with respect to the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease. To some extent conditions are changing from day to day.
The minister's statement that we have had discussion on these matters in the past-and [at- this moment it is many months in the past

-surely does not put us in the position where we should not be able to ask questions of ministers and receive answers from them in respect of any subject appearing in the supplementary estimates. We should have the ministers here for that purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If we have an extended discussion on every item in the supplementary estimates in respect of every department, then I suggest it makes the business of parliament nearly impossible. I can give my hon. friend any information he wants as to how the $665,000 is being spent. I have the data before me. But I do suggest this is not the time to embark upon a discussion of the principle of compensation for these contagious diseases.
We have already had considerable discussion in the matter, and we are bound to have much more. There has been talk about amending the rules of the house; but, for heaven's sake, if we cannot exercise some measure of self-control in debate, there is not much use talking about amending the rules.
The minister's answer to my colleague from Calgary East is most inappropriate at this time. Here we have a vote in respect of something never before considered in our history.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It relates to more than foot-and-mouth disease, I may say.

We have questioned the minister about the basis of payment. That matter had not been settled. A board was set up under the legislation to arrive at a basis of settlement. It was a month ago today the session opened. Several of us have asked the Minister of Agriculture whether a basis of settlement has been arrived at, and he has answered that it has not, but that when it was done he would make a statement to the house explaining the basis of payment for the herds that must be destroyed. I am very much disappointed the minister is not here to answer those questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not quarrel with that too much. I am ready to allow the item to stand, and we will have the minister here later. But I do feel that we cannot do this on every item, or we will just never finish our work. In respect of this item I can see there may be a number of cogent questions hon. members might wish to ask.
Let it stand. But there are several items, and we cannot allow them all to stand.
The hon. member for Greenwood has made it clear that we would not be discussing all of them.

speechtext: Stands.

Mr. Chairman, I have allowed other members to speak, but I wish to speak now because this is a very-important item, so far as my constituency is concerned.
I have not opposed the payment of full compensation in respect of foot-and-mouth disease, but I must point out that people in Nova Scotia have suffered greatly because of the existence of that disease in western Canada, because of the embargo placed upon the shipment of meat products.
I have risen to say that in Nova Scotia we have a complaint against the health of animals branch. I brought the matter up in the house on December 29, at which time I received only a partial reply from the Minister of Agriculture. I agree with the hon. member for Moose Jaw, the hon. member for Souris and other members, that it is most surprising-indeed, it seems to me there must have been some plan or scheme- that the Minister of Agriculture or his assistant could not be present this afternoon to give even a small amount of information on an expenditure amounting to $665,000.
It is amazing that this should be the case. In fact, it is almost an insult to members of the House of Commons, and to members in the opposition to whom an appeal is made to allow these items to pass-. The hon, member for Greenwood has said that we are not going to hold up the items, but that we do want certain fundamental information.
At this time I am going to refer to Newcastle disease in Nova Scotia, and I make a direct charge against the health of animals branch in respect of the recommendations it made, and the encouragement it gave to the owners of hatcheries in Nova Scotia-I believe there were eleven hatcheries directly affected-to use these vaccines. The department sent down live vaccine which, instead of preventing the disease, inoculated all these hatcheries.
The $4,400,000 voted last year is increased this year to $4,889,000. The poultry users of Nova Scotia received from the branch the vaccines that brought this dangerous disease into Nova Scotia. The branch admits that the flocks were inoculated hy the vaccine * from the branch, and- yet we are now- asked to vote it a large sum of money.
I should like now to read briefly from a report, I-received about tep-days ago. I- stall

not read the whole of it, but the pertinent part is as follows:
An inactivated vaccine was prepared and released by this department on request to the provinces who assumed the responsibility for vaccination.
Field evidence suggests that the vaccine caused this disease, since with the exception of two flocks the disease appeared only in vaccinated flocks.

Partly used ii these hatcheries in Nova Scotia by government officials-

It is the intention of the department to complete investigations at the earliest moment possible in consultation with the province and determine responsibilities, if any, to flock owners.
Will consideration be given to the payment of compensation for the damages suffered by these hatcheries? I have a letter here from one of the hatcheries, dated March 20, which reads:
They did not instruct us to vaccinate, but they strongly advised doing so, and assured us that there would be no after effects. We feel therefore that it is their responsibility to pay for the losses caused by using the vaccine.
I would also like to inform you regarding the official report of the House of Commons, on Friday. March 14, where you brought up Newcastle disease, where in reply to your question Hon. J. G. Gardiner said that compensation has been paid to owners of flocks for birds and eggs destroyed for the purpose of controlling Newcastle disease. I would like to advise you that to date not one cent of compensation of any kind has been received by myself, or my brother, and I have been told by good authority that the Pictou county farmers have not received any compensation either. I think this matter should be brought to the attention of the house, as they cannot expect farmers to go back into the poultry business without money to do so, and it is not fair that they should have to undergo hardships due to lack of money because of their losses with Newcastle disease.
I have received letters from other hatcheries. On March 19 a question which had been asked by the hon. member for Anna-polis-Kings was answered, as reported on page 586 of Hansard. The questions and answers are as follows:

I demand that the small hatcheries in Nova Scotia should receive compensation. The amount of compensation that would be paid is small in comparison with what has been paid in the west. These men have sent in their accounts which have been before the department for months. I brought up this matter in December last but I did not discuss it at any length because we did not want to give unnecessary publicity to this great menace.
This great poultry industry has been built up in recent years until today it has an output valued at $10 million a year. However, the householders are so alarmed about the danger of using birds or eggs from these districts that they have stopped buying. This matter is exceedingly important and I urge that full compensation be paid. These men have sent in their accounts and they are entitled to a reply. We have passed legislation giving full and adequate compensation to the farmers and stock raisers who have suffered from foot-and-mouth disease, and I appeal to the committee to see that the same treatment is given to these hatcheries in Nova Scotia.
It is true that we are only a small province; it is true that we are shoved to one side on every possible occasion, but here is a case where fair and reasonable compensation should be paid in relation to what is being paid in Saskatchewan for foot-and-mouth disease. I consider it the duty of the Minister of Agriculture and his officials to see that adequate compensation is paid, especially when we are being appealed to to pass other large items for compensation. I am not going to hold up the item, but I do want an answer as to when this compensation will be paid.

I should like to ask a question on item 572. Do the immigrants who have been brought here since the end of December 31, from the United Kingdom, include personnel who are not citizens of the United Kingdom, people who might be described as displaced persons coming from Europe, or are they all United Kingdom citizens?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
They are not all
United Kingdom citizens. When the scheme was started, it was announced as a scheme to aid the migration here of people from the British isles, having in mind the fact that transportation was lacking to a greater extent from the United Kingdom than it was from continental Europe. There have come from the United Kingdom people who were not United Kingdom citizens.

Then I should like to make this observation. Owing to the fact that at this season of the year, that is between December 31 and April 1, there has been a considerable amount of unemployment in Canada, and that unemployment has been aggravated by bringing those people who are not even British subjects from Europe by air and distributing them across Canada. I do not think it is a proper expenditure.
It so happens that during the month of January I paid a visit to an immigration centre and I saw about 100 young Europeans, some of whom had only just arrived while others had been there for three months. They were being maintained at the expense of the Canadian taxpayer while the Department of Citizenship- and Immigration was trying to' hunt up jobs for them. They had no particular appointment to come to. These individuals had arrived, and they had to be fed and housed by the department. The department was sending out its field men to get employment for them, and at the same time competing with our labour department which was endeavouring to find jobs for Canadian citizens who were also unemployed. It seems to me that this has been an extremely foolish thing to do, and now we are voting extra money to bring these European youths to this country by air instead of letting them wait until there was an opportunity to bring them by boat. In this way they would have

arrived at a time when there would have been an opportunity for work and they would not have had to be kept. We are not only paying the difference between sea passage and air passage; we are also maintaining them all these winter months.
Why was it necessary to speed up the arrival of these people in this country? Why was it necessary to bring them by air instead of waiting until they could take sea passage in the normal course of events?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: There was no speeding up during the winter months. On the contrary, there were fewer who came forward.
There was a speeding up because they were brought by air instead of waiting until they could get passage by ship in three months' time.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Perhaps we are disagreeing about the use of words. I understood the hon. member to refer to the speeding up of immigration during the winter months. If all he means is that the normal flow of immigrants should have been reduced under those circumstances during the three months, that is a different matter; but I understood him to say we had speeded up immigration during the winter months by the use of this scheme, and that is not the case. The air scheme was continued as it had been a year ago. It must be remembered that this program began on December 1, 1950, and has been continued since that time. It was carried on during the winter months a year ago with no consequences such as those to which the hon. member now refers. I take it that the camp to which he is referring was Victoria.
Yes, that is the one I saw.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
It is correct, Mr. Chairman, to say that we had a number in Victoria during the winter months. There are thirteen there today, which shows that we have been reasonably successful in placing these people during the winter months. I am free to admit that anyone could make out a case for closing down immigration on October 1 and opening it again on April 1, if he wished to do so. Experience has shown you just cannot do that. It is true that you must be careful, and you should not flood the market during the winter months particularly, because seasonal unemployment will occur in Canada every winter. It may well be that we should have seen that fewer people came this winter in particular industries, but I suggest to the house, as a fact, that at no time during those winter months have we had more than roughly 2,000 workers at any time throughout our camps in Canada;

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration that is not a large number considering the fact that we find 190,000 people came here during 1951.
Admittedly there have been some difficulties and we have overcome them pretty well. I suggest, however, that an immigration program based on a six-month period is not possible nor is it desirable because the farming community needs their workers on April 1 and up until July 15. We have been bringing out farm workers throughout the winter months, and there are none of them that I know of in our hostels at the moment.
Does this apply only to farm workers?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: I did not mean to convey that impression. I was giving that as an example of the fact that you must maintain some immigration during the winter months. I could add that you must bring dependents because there are more dependents abroad than there should be, in the minds of those here who are waiting for them; and the fall and the winter season is a proper time to bring them here, if your transportation is short for the workers in the summer season.
As this was quite a burning question in British Columbia in the early months of this year,-

I should like to ask the minister a question, but before doing so I should like to say that I certainly cannot agree with what the hon. member for Nanaimo just said. If there is one department of the government that I think is really functioning, it is the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. I think the figures speak for themselves and I hope the minister will keep up the good work. The question I should like to ask is this, and I may say that I have had several inquiries from my constituents. It concerns Canadians who stayed in England after the war, married English girls and who now have not the funds to come back to Canada, but wish to do so. Is there any way in which they can get this kind of assisted passage?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
The purpose of the assisted passage was to promote immigration to Canada. Speaking strictly offhand, I would suppose that that was intended to cover a person who was not entitled to come

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration to Canada as of right. The Canadian citizen resident abroad may return as of right. Nevertheless, if there is a problem there which my hon. friend has in mind, I shall be glad if he will let me know about it, and we will consider the question of whether one could use the assisted passage scheme for the returning Canadian.

I have no fault at all to find with the policy of the government in bringing in 200,000 immigrants a year. The fault I find is with the way these immigrants are handled once they arrive in Canada. As far as I can make out-and I have spent some time getting information on this matter-it seems that the government has based its policy on the idea that you can bring these immigrants to Canada, simply dump them into the labour market and assume that they are going to be able to fend for themselves from then on. As a result of the many contacts that I have made with these people, I can say that they are just not able to do that. The natural result of this policy is that many	industries-especially agriculturewhich badly need workers are still exceedingly short while cities, such as my own city of Toronto, have been swamped with these immigrants during the winter months, from November until the present time, and those immigrants simply become a load on the taxpayers. The ones that have obtained a job have usually done so at the expense of Canadian workmen because, coming from Europe, they have been accustomed to a lower standard of living and are willing to accept employment at wages lower than the going Canadian rate of wage.
Another thing which this unplanned policy of immigration has done-and which has resulted in the flocking of these immigrants to the cities-is that it has caused a tremendous upset in connection with the housing problem in cities such as Toronto and many others across the country, especially at a time when the government's policy of cutting out their one-sixth mortgage loan and increasing the interest rate on National Housing Act has decreased the number of houses started in this country during the last twelve months by 24 per cent. This has caused an intolerable situation, especially in cities. I think that one of the things this government has got to realize is that an immigrant without a job is not an asset to the country, but is, instead, a liability.
I believe that these immigrants should be brought in to fill specific jobs for which there is a shortage of Canadian workmen and not simply to swell the ranks of the


unemployed, as has been the situation during the last year, in a great number of cases. If these people are brought in to a specific job where they are needed and if they are kept at that job for a minimum of one year or possibly two, I believe that at the end of that time they will have learned the language, will probably have learned to like their surroundings and the job that they are working at, and in all probability will stay at it instead of simply flocking to the cities and aggravating the problems of unemployment and housing which already exist in those cities.
If the government wants to make a success of this policy of immigration, I think they should give consideration to bringing people in to specific jobs and require them to stay for a certain length of time. If they do that, I think they will find that these people will stay there, that these industries that need workers will get them. In addition, I think the people who come in will be happier. There will not be nearly as many drifters. The immigration policy will then be one which will contribute to the productivity and the growth of this country instead of being in the chaotic condition which I believe it is in today.
I do not intend to make a speech, Mr. Chairman; I want to ask some questions. Like the hon. member for Moose Jaw I agree with the government's immigration policy. The figure was 200,000, was it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration

speechtext: I think it should have been 394,000. That is the only quarrel I have with it. I believe it should have been larger. I am interested in the inspection of those coming in here, and I refer to the situation in the province of British Columbia with respect to the municipalities. I am not now talking about young men. The municipalities are unfortunately being called upon to care for these people. It is the municipalities that are being called upon to do this, not the provincial government and not the federal government which brought them here. It is the poor little farm owner in the municipality who must shoulder the burden. Immigrants come in at the age of 65 or over. I should like the minister to explain who is going to care for those people. Are you going to expect individual municipalities to continue doing that?
I wonder if the minister would not consider setting up distributing centres for immigration?
Might I first have an answer to my question?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: In answer to the question asked by the hon. member for Fraser Valley, may I say that it is not often that a person over 65 is admitted to Canada. In general the policy is to point out that opportunities are available here for those of younger years. It may well be that the case which my hon. friend has in mind is that of a parent of a Canadian citizen. If that is the case, I would suppose that, upon application by the child for the parent, an engagement would be given to provide housing, to maintain the parent and so on, if the parent were not able to look after himself. That may not be the case, but I would think it probably is. If the hon. member will give me the details, I shall look into the matter. If there is an obligation on the child, I am sure that the child should have that obligation drawn to his attention.

The reason I am talking about inspection is this. I will mention one case, not by name, in which there must be slackness somewhere. I understand that the child or the relative is supposed to care for these people. But I can refer to one case- and for ten years I had certain municipal experience-where the relative was on relief all the time. He learned that racket of relief. This immigrant I would say was 60 years of age and over-
What is the name?

Oh no, I am not going to give the name. You would not want your constituent's name put on the record, and I am not going to put this one on. I will give the minister the name in private. I want to know what the policy is. Are the municipalities going to be called upon to bear the burden if the son or daughter is on relief and falls down on his or her obligations? I think immigration should be limited to western Canada. I do not think it is good policy to take some thousands of these people and place them in the province of Ontario, for instance, or in the cities of Quebec when in the west we have large areas where they could settle and make their way. Up in northeastern British Columbia there is a need for a definite policy with regard to handling these immigrants. I suggest that the government consider a distributing centre
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration where groups of these people coming in could pause and wait a few days or a few weeks until work is provided for them or until they are able to acquire some land to find their way around. At the present time no provision is made for these newcomers. Naturally they find things difficult, coming as they do into a strange country, not knowing the language and knowing little about the geography of the country. There is a problem there. I consider that the railways should co-operate with the government of Canada in setting up some sort of hostels, particularly up in the Peace river country, where families could be housed' and kept for a few days or a few weeks until work was found for them. I might say that there is plenty of employment available up in that part of the country, particularly for agricultural people. The number of people being brought over from Europe should be increased. It must be obvious to this house that we are spending many millions of dollars for military and economic support to those countries over there in Europe. There is no more humane or more sensible way of assisting them than by taking some of the surplus population from that war-ridden part of the earth up into western Canada, and giving them a chance to have their own land and to build houses. I think the minister is doing a good job, but he should have more support. There should be just a little more planning in respect to placing settlers in western Canada.

I do not wish to enter into any debate on the question of immigration. I imagine there will be time later on to discuss immigration. After listening to the remarks, one would think that quantity was what was wanted in this country in so far as immigration was concerned; whereas I think quality is more important than quantity. Eut that is something we can discuss later.
My reason for rising now is to ask the minister whether he is making the most of the facilities which he has at the different ports in Canada for dealing with immigrants. I ask this question as the result of a return which I received the other day, and which indicated that out of some 200,000 immigrants brought into Canada last year only 6,000 came in through the port of Saint John. I am told that in the port of Saint John we have one of the finest immigration sheds not only in Canada but anywhere in North America. It does seem to me that in view of the fine facilities we have in Saint John, 6,000 immigrants out of 200,000 coming to the country is just a mere trickle.
A moment ago an hon. member said something about not bringing immigrants in, in

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the winter months. The only immigrants who come to Saint John come in the winter months of December, January and February. In addition to having these fine facilities, Saint John is a year-round port. I do not believe that the minister's department is making the proper use of these fine facilities. Cannot more use be made of the facilities that exist in the port of Saint John?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: I was most surprised when I saw the return to my hon. friend. I shall be glad to look into the question of whether a better way can be found of using the facilities at Saint John to a greater extent than the return indicated.
They have very fine facilities.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Oh, yes.

What measure of control has the minister over immigrants coming to this country for farm labour purposes? I have had letters, sometimes twice a week, from farmers who have applied for an immigrant. They have got them over to this country and the immigrants have stayed probably two or three weeks or a month and then left. Sometimes the farmers say that they are quite satisfied with the work of the immigrant, but apparently the immigrant simply uses the application by the farmer as a vehicle to get into this country, and once he gets here he gets away to the city as fast as he can. This is a problem in my constituency, particularly to the dairy farmers. These farmers apply for a man, counting on him to do some work, and then they are left without any person to help. I had one letter from a very up-to-date farmer who is operating a rather large dairy farm. He pointed out that owing to the trouble in getting labour it was becoming too hard for himself, his wife and his family to continue. He cited the troubles he had in bringing people to this country to work for him. He mentioned making application to the department, and then the man would leave and he would be in trouble again. I have had several letters on this matter, and I should like the minister to tell me what measure of control he has over these people. When a farmer makes application and the immigrant comes in and is accepted, what can be done to make him carry out his part of the bargain?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
There are two kinds of farm immigration. There is the immigration under what was the IRO, administered by the Department of Labour, and the immigration under the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. Under the former an engagement was taken with the person who came by the assistance of the
IMr. Brooks.]

IRO that he would remain in employment for a year. There have been many occasions in the house when the question of persons leaving under those conditions had been brought to the attention of the former minister of labour, but not so much to the later one. My impression of that was that every effort was made to see that the farm worker carried out his contract. I do not know of any instances when persuasion went beyond that.
In the case of immigration, we do not have a contract, but I am open to the suggestion that we should have one. Nevertheless, hon. members ought to bear this in mind. There are great disadvantages in trying to maintain the relationship of employer and employee when one or the other does not want it; and it can be argued that we should not go in for a form of forced labour, as that would be under certain conditions. I quite realize that that is not a satisfactory answer to the farmer who, in the midst of the haying season, loses the man that he thought was going to stay with him for the season. At the same time, we have discussed this with farm representatives time and time again, and they are not unanimous that there should be anything more than there is in the way of persuasion of the worker. I know it is frustrating, and certainly, as far as the department is concerned, we frown upon it as much as we can. We have sent our placement officers time and time again to these people asking them not to leave, when they have given notice. We point out to them the obligation that they have to stay throughout the period of time, and in many cases it succeeds. However, many farmers who have lost their farm workers come to us and say: Well, if he does not want to stay we had better let him go. Get me another one, and we will do our best under those conditions.

I might say that we too had an immigrant come to our place a year ago. I obtained him through the minister. He came direct from Holland, and a very fine specimen he is. I do not think that we ever had a better man around our place. I used this method of keeping him there because of the fact that he was suitable and we liked him very much. When he came to make arrangements with me as to what money he was to get I said to him: "Do you need money?" He said: "No, I do not, but I just wondered how much I was going to get." Owing to the fact that I was not at home myself, that conversation went on for a month or two before this happened, and we had plenty of time to know whether we liked him or not. This is what happened. Instead of trying to talk to him-he could not speak English very well, but he can

speak pretty well now-I took a lead pencil and a piece of paper, and I started him off on a low wage and I raised it $5 a month until the end of the year, which finally brought him up to $100 a month. I passed the paper back to him. I said: "This is more money than you asked for." I asked him first what wages he expected to get. He said, "I think I should get $70 a month." I said, "All right." Then I gave him this paper with the wage scale on it. It was a low wage to start with and then it was built up by $5 a month for twelve months. He is still with me. There have been no complaints one way or the other. He is a very fine chap, and as long as I can keep him there he is going to stay with me.
If you keep on giving him $5 a month indefinitely it will be very profitable for him.

The point I tried to make, whether I made myself clear or not, is this. The fact of the matter is I started him off at $50 a month. He wanted $70. I said that if he wanted to stay there and earn high wages then it was up to him. If he wanted to move any place else, he could do so, but I started him off at the low wage.

Has the minister or his department, or any department of the government, had any conversations or communications with the British government with regard to the amount of assets which the English settler coming to Canada can bring in? We are losing many good settlers who are going to Australia and New Zealand because they can take the pounds that they have there, while they have to exchange pounds for dollars when they come to Canada. The British government, of course, is short of dollars. I was wondering whether the government has had any conversation recently with the British government with regard to this matter, or whether they were prepared themselves to accept the British pounds from some of these immigrants and give them our Canadian dollars-when they come to Canada. It seems to me that we could very well give some consideration to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration

speechtext: Over what period?

speechtext: I thought it was four years, but the parliamentary assistant to the minister of finance says three years.

I sympathize with the minister regarding his difficulty in trying to formulate a satisfactory contract between the farm worker and the farmer. I doubt whether it would be possible to settle on such a contract, because if the farm worker is not satisfied with the conditions under which he is working, then if you tried to keep him there it would mean he would be a nuisance to the farmer. He would be better off elsewhere.
What I rose to say was that I hope the minister will not do anything to slow down the bringing of farm workers to this country. In the next few weeks there will be an urgent need for farm help in western Canada. The harvest was not completed; and unless it can be completed before seeding begins there may be serious loss.
No doubt there will be tremendous demand for farm help in the western provinces just as soon as the land is dry enough. Most farmers will be quite prepared to accept farm help several days or perhaps weeks before the harvest actually begins. The kind of farm help needed today, however, is quite different from that needed in the past. Today farming is a highly mechanized operation. Therefore the minister should try to bring to this country as many as possible of those who are used to farm machinery.
We realize that there may be some difficulty, in view of the fact that the men who are used to handling farm machinery would be qualified to get jobs elsewhere at higher wages. That is. especially true in Alberta where we have oil drilling operations. The oil drillers are offering much higher wages than prevail on the farm, thus making it difficult to keep the men who go to the farms. I certainly hope the minister will do all he can to expedite the bringing of farm workers to this country.

I have a dozen questions I should like to put to the minister. I appreciate there will be other opportunities to discuss immigration, but I think these questions could be answered now. They are of interest to a number of people across Canada.
Would the minister state briefly the general departmental idea in connection with selective or planned immigration-and I believe those are the words used when the


subject of immigration is discussed. Is planning done with relation to jobs available in Canada, or areas in Canada that might require immigrants? Is planning done in relation to the various countries supplying the immigrants?

The ages are 28 and 26 respectively. I should like to draw the attention of the minister to one or two matters which I have passed on to him in the last month or two. The first concerns two young Chinese who made formal application to come to Canada before they had reached the age of 25 years. I understand that in both cases they were suitable from health and other standpoints. However, there was delay in processing the applications through Vancouver and Hong Kong with the result that by the time approval reached Ottawa the
(Mr. Harris (Grey-Bruce).]

birthdays of both boys had occurred and technically they were too old to be admitted.
It seems to me that in these cases the same principle should be applied as is applied in the case of old age pension applications. The old age pension is paid from the date the application is received in Ottawa. If such had been the case these applications for entrance would have been approved and these boys could have been admitted. As their families live in Canada I think it is most unfair that because of delay in either Hong Kong or Vancouver, delay which was not their fault, they are not to be admitted. I urge the minister to consider changing the act or the interpretation to provide that the date official applications are received in Ottawa will be the date that applies.
The other matter concerns Chinese who visit China and stay over the permitted period of two years. When they return to Canada they find they must wait five or six years before they are eligible for Canadian citizenship. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is an item on which, as I indicated the other day, I should like to make a brief statement.
When I tabled the further supplementary estimates the other day hon. members will recall that I also tabled a report on the actuarial examination of the civil service
Supply-Finance
superannuation account in the consolidated revenue fund for the period of March 31, 1931, to December 31, 1947. At that time I promised to make a statement on that report when the time came to discuss the items in these supplementary estimates which are concerned with the policy which the government proposes to follow in making its contributions as an employer to the superannuation account.
The department of insurance have made two actuarial examinations or valuations since the account was set up in 1924. The whole purpose of such a valuation is to make an actuarial estimate of the total liability and to determine if the balance in the account is sufficient to meet that liability. If it is not sufficient, we have a deficit which means that adequate provision has not been made for the payment of our liabilities.
Hon. members may recall that a year agcr parliament was asked to vote $75 million to reduce the deficit in this account. I then indicated that there was every reason to expect that the deficit would be several times that figure and this is now confirmed by the report. At December 31, 1947, the estimated total liability was $341,149,000 and the balance in the account amounted to $89,544,000 leaving a deficit of $251,605,000. I have since been advised by the chief actuary of the department of insurance that, by December 31, 1951, the total liability had increased to an estimated $509 million while the amount standing to the credit of the account had increased to $197 million. The deficit had thus increased to an estimated $312 million at December 31, 1951, even after the special contribution made a year ago.
Since the report was submitted1 to me it has been carefully studied in order to determine what should be done to reduce the existing deficit and to prevent the creation of a new one. In my later remarks I shall outline certain changes in policy and later in this session I shall introduce a bill to amend the act to take care of other aspects of this problem.
I should point out that the Civil Service Superannuation Act does not provide specifically for government payments except the payment of interest on the balance in the account but other contributions are implicitly required sooner or later if the various benefits; are to be paid. It had been the practice to do no more than pay the required amount of interest and match the contributions of the employees for current service from 1924 until the vote of $75 million a year ago.
The actuarial report states quite clearly that the deficit is caused almost entirely by two main factors. The first arose from the fact

Supply-Finance
that the government matched only the contributions of employees for their current 'service and not those made for their prior service. Government contributions should be made for both types to cover the full liability. Secondly, the contribution rates are calculated on the basis of a normal progression up the established salary scales so that when there is [DOT]a general salary increase the contributions already made are actually inadequate relative to the larger pension which will be received and the over-all liability is increased. Up to the present no payment has been made ,in respect of such an increase.
These factors were responsible for the estimated deficit of $53 million at March 31, 1933, which I mentioned in my statement a year ago. Unfortunately the government of the day felt itself unable to take steps to correct the situation and the matter was allowed to run on until the war came. Then early in 1947 with the first amendment of the act after the war the situation was reviewed and was felt to be so changed that the department of insurance was asked to make preparations for this new valuation which is based on data at the end of that year.
It will be apparent from their report that these factors which I have mentioned have operated with increasing intensity since the end of the war. There has recently been a large increase in unmatched contributions in respect of prior service and several increases in the general level of salaries. Although contribution rates were raised in 1939 new benefits have been introduced1 and retired civil servants are living longer. The combination of all these factors has been to greatly increase the deficit of 1933.
We propose to continue the policy initiated by the vote of $75 million a year ago and to wipe out the accumulated deficit over a reasonable period. Vote 586 of these supplementary estimates constitutes an additional appropriation of the same amount for the same purpose.
Secondly, I am proposing to show on our government balance sheet the full estimated actuarial liability of the superannuation fund at the end of each fiscal year, with an appropriate offset for the deficit which still exists. It is also proposed to credit to the account each year in future an amount equal to interest reckoned at the same four per cent rate as in the past but calculated on the amount of the full actuarial liability; this will prevent the present deficit from growing owing to a loss of interest.
Thirdly, in vote 584 for $4,943,977 the government is taking the first step in a policy
tMr. Abbott.]
it proposes of matching not only the contributions made by contributors for current service but also for prior service.
Further, the government proposes to make a special contribution to the account of an amount estimated by the department of insurance to be equal to the additional net liability created by any general salary increase. The actuarial cost to the account of the general salary increases effective December 1, 1951, is estimated at $23 million and vote 585 is proposed to cover that cost.
Before concluding this explanation, I might point out to hon. members the ultimate purpose behind these major appropriations. Our pension plan with its various benefits is an integral and essential part of the pay that is provided for civil servants. It is taken into account in establishing salary rates and other conditions of employment. It is, I think, wholly fitting that part of the remuneration of persons in the public service should take this form, because the security that a pension plan provides helps to ensure that independence and stability which is so important in the public service. To many of those in it, the public service cannot offer financial rewards on the scale that they could secure in commercial, industrial, or professional life; rather it offers that interest and satisfaction which arise from the nature of the work and the purposes to which it is directed. If we are to expect many of the persons in the public service to carry on under these circumstances we must, I think, provide them with reasonable security for their old age or disability so that they can to that degree disregard the necessity for seeking immediate financial gains. The appropriations which we are proposing are intended to bring fully into focus these accumulated and accruing obligations, in order that the full cost of carrying on the busines of government will be revealed in our appropriations and accounts.

well known, Mr. Speaker, that I am just as sincere in my opposition to divorce as any man in this house, but I think that this is a discredit to the House of Commons-
