speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) noted that one of his remarks was greeted with enthusiastic applause from all sections of the house. I have no doubt it was greeted with applause by members of his own party just because they are of his own party, but on this side of the house we agree to the full with his statement that this whole business is a farce and a discredit to parliament, and in my view we should get rid of it just as soon as we possibly can. I submit that what I have been trying to do with respect to these bills, namely to have them deferred until we get the evidence, is no reflection of any kind on the other place or upon the members of the committee in the other place. I have no doubt that with respect to Bill No. 12, which was letter G of the Senate, the members of the Senate committee went into it fully. But in this House of Commons we were not eleoted by the people of Canada to be a rubber stamp. We were not sent here to take without looking at it any matter that

is laid before us. I think it is our responsibility to have in our hands, even if some members do not want to read it, the evidence in connection with this case and with the other cases before we go ahead with them.
1 dislike voting on these divorce cases one way or the other. As some hon. members are suggesting, once these people have paid their fees and have gone through the routine that is required, they have a certain right. But I submit that they also have the right to have this sort of matter dealt with somewhere else than in parliament. I feel that we have got to face up to that fact just as soon as possible. For the moment, however, that question is not before us, Mr. Speaker. You have ruled that we must deal with the bill that is in our hands. What we have now before us is Bill No. 12, an act for the relief of a certain person. I submit that, with no evidence and no information about this case other than the name of the petitioner and the name of the person against whom the charge of adultery is made, we should wait until we have the evidence. Believing that it is the responsible thing for a member of this house to do in this circumstance, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), that the debate on the motion for second reading of Bill No. 12 be now adjourned.

584. To provide for a government contribution to the superannuation fund in an amount equal to the estimated current and arrears payments of individual contributors in the previous fiscal year- further amount required, $4,943,977.

Mr. Chairman, before six o'clock we had an interesting statement from the Minister of Finance as to the nature and purpose of this vote. The fact had emerged that the intention of the government is to place the civil service superannuation fund on an up-to-date actuarial basis. But there was one thing which I do not think had been established clearly, and therefore I should like to ask the minister whether I am correct in my understanding that although this is, in the sense in which he explained it, a bookkeeping transaction, the effect nevertheless will be that when he gives us his completed statement of revenues and expenditures at the time he presents his budget the net surplus will have been reduced by the total of $102,943,977, as a result of votes 584, 585 and 586; so that that reduction will be reflected when he presents his official report on the surplus.

Supply-Finance

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is quite correct. My budgetary surplus, if any, which I shall report at the end of the fiscal year, will be $102,943,977 less than it would otherwise be.

Then, Mr. Chairman, is it also correct that, notwithstanding the fact that, on paper, this sum of $102 million has been transferred from what I understand would otherwise be the budgetary surplus, to the civil service superannuation account, nevertheless that amount still remains in the consolidated revenue fund?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The superannuation account, as my hon. friend is doubtless aware, is an account in the consolidated revenue fund; and this is one of the items. There are no securities or investments held against the superannuation funds. It is an account in the consolidated revenue fund. And, as I have had occasion to explain on a number of occasions, this is one of the non-cash items in budgetary income and outgo. There are others of the same kind. There are cash receipts, on the other hand, which are not budgetary receipts, and the cash represented by the revenues have, of course, been used in part in the way I outlined in the radio speech to which the hon. member for Greenwood has referred.
There is no mystery about it. I never attempted to place it before the house in any other way. This is a perfectly well-known budgetary charge, in the same way that there are others of a similar type.

I hope the minister will understand that I am not suggesting that the books will not reflect proper entries, or that there has been any attempt to mislead the house and country. But it is important to establish the facts of the case. I should like, then, arising out of the previous two questions and answers, to ask the minister if I am correct in understanding that, as he himself has said in the radio speech to which he made reference earlier, in which he described ways in which the budgetary surplus would be used- that the budgetary surplus could be used for certain things such as the retirement of debt -am I correct in thinking that the actual cash on hand could be used for the retirement of debt, to the full extent of the budgetary surplus, and yet leave leeway for the transfer of this amount, which is not cash but merely a paper figure, from the unappropriated total in the consolidated revenue fund to the civil service superannuation fund?
So that there will be no suggestion that I am trying to twist words or trying to lay a trap-I am not very good at laying traps- what I am getting at is this; Is it possible that this entry, although the cash is paid out

in retirement of debt, can, as it were, be used twice, and a paper entry still be made so as to show a payment into the civil service superannuation fund?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, it cannot be used twice, any more than cash can be used twice. Cash is taken in as the result of receipts from taxes, from non-tax revenue, and other sources- interest on investments, and so on. And that cash is used for the purposes approved by parliament, including the redemption of debt.
If it seems in the public interest to use surplus cash to reduce either short-term or long-term debt, the debit entry, the budgetary debit, which will result from the item we are now discussing will be a charge to the budgetary revenue account and will be credited to the superannuation account.
As I said, and as my hon. friend has said, no cash changes hands in that entry, and the resulting cash may be used, as I have said, in the manner outlined in my radio speech. The obligation remains there to pay as and when these pensions become due as a result of claims of civil servants. It is a perfectly common, ordinary, everyday sort of transaction. There is nothing mysterious about it at all.

That is correct, there is nothing mysterious about it; but the effect of it is that, although he is able to show that the budgetary surplus has been reduced by the amount of this appropriation, nevertheless that much in cash has been available and may already have been used, according to the minister's radio speech, to retire debt. The cash there has been used to retire debt, but here is a paper entry of another $102 million. It seems to me that somehow or another in one case we have used money for one purpose and then, on paper, made a book entry, which does not mean we are using the money again, but that the same amount is used for the purposes of the book entry. And, in effect, it is being used-or the same figure is being used-twice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, I am not an accountant, although in the course of my professional experience I used to have a good deal to do with figures. I have tried to make the situation clear. I said time and again in my budget speech of last year that the budgetary surplus had no direct relationship to cash surplus; and it may well be-in fact it frequently would be the case-that a fairly substantial budgetary surplus might mean that we would be running at the same time a cash deficit, because of other non-budgetary obligations.
Now, I always make perfectly clear in my annual budget speech how the full intake of

revenue has been used, and the extent to which it has been used for non-budgetary items. And I always bring into account nonbudgetary receipts. It is in accordance with well recognized and well understood accounting balance-sheet practices. I am afraid I cannot elaborate upon it further.

I must admit, as a private member, that I was rather surprised to see this staggering figure placed before us.
I have one or two suggestions to make to the Minister of Finance. If I understood correctly, civil servants have the option of retiring any time after reaching the age of sixty. They must retire-they are compelled to retire-upon reaching the age of sixty-five. Any figures I have seen would seem to indicate that most of them wait until that time. Therefore I would assume that they would prefer not to retire when they reach the age of sixty-five, or would like to wait until they are older.
I am going to suggest to the minister and the committee that this policy, which has been accepted by the government and parliament, of retiring civil servants at sixty-five has become outdated and outmoded. I think it is financially unsound, and for several reasons. In the first place I do not think most civil servants like this idea of being retired compulsorily because, after all, with the cost of living as it is, even if they want to retire they find it difficult to live on their pensions.
In the second place I think that retiring civil servants at the age of sixty-five is harming the production of the country. After all, when we are in the midst of a defence effort, I do not see how we can have men at the top dropping out of the civil service. Men who have reached the age of sixty-five have experience which makes them most valuable.
In the third place I think the policy is ill-advised because it is costing the taxpayers an unnecessary amount of money. They are being forced to pay for retirement pensions of civil servants who are rendered unproductive, usually through no fault of their own.
Therefore I suggest to the minister that he give consideration to changing the Civil Service Act so that the civil servant might not have to retire. If a civil servant wishes to retire, all right; but if he wishes to continue working he should be allowed to continue to work until reaching the age of perhaps sixty-eight. I think everyone would benefit from this arrangement-the civil servant, the country as a whole, and certainly the taxpayer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have great sympathy with the views expressed by the hon. member. I
Supply-Finance
do not know whether he was in the house this afternoon when I mentioned that we are bringing in the Civil Service Superannuation Act for complete revision at this session. It is hoped that general observations relating to superannuation, and benefits of that sort, might be made at that time-and perhaps more properly then.

I should like to add a word to what has been said by the hon, member for Moose Jaw, because I believe I have roughly the same thought. It seems to me that there are two points involved. First of all I noticed from reading the minister's memorandum that a certain number of people-I do not know how many- are retiring at sixty. That seems to me very undesirable, except in special cases. As the hon. member for Moose Jaw has said, it costs a lot of money. The minister shakes his head -well, perhaps he will explain in some further detail. I should have thought that, in the same way as stopping people from working at sixty-five as against a later age would cost the public money, stopping them before sixty-five would cost money, too.
I would add one further word to what the hon. member for Moose Jaw has said, and it is this: It seems to me the practical way of approaching the matter might be to have the age of sixty-five as the more or less normal retiring age, but to allow the heads of departments to recommend that, in proper cases, they might remain longer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the case now.
It is?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. Every week we have
extensions beyond sixty-five.
Up to what age?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no deadline. There has to be a certificate that they are essential for the purpose of the service.

Then, just
one or two other points. As I listened to the minister referring to our deficit in 1947 of $251 million, and of $312 million at the end of 1951, as against actuarial perfection it seems to me that we are like people on a treadmill-running as fast as we can, but the treadmill is working faster, and we are actually losing ground, even though we have transferred an amount of money to try to keep up the actuarial position. The point of age has been dealt with and that to me is a most important matter. As the minister says the whole thing will be reviewed in the near future, I think this is all I have to say.

Supply-Finance

I should like to ask some questions with reference to these three votes. With the huge surplus the minister has I think he could have worked in something for those underprivileged people who have to live on retirement allowances of some $25 per month. Now that the funds are available the minister has a real opportunity to give these people at least a cost of living bonus. Many civil servants have been retired on allowances of $29, $39 and $79 a month.
This question has been up a dozen times. While I have no objection to civil servants getting an increase, I am thinking of the man who has been in the civil service and is retired. There is in my riding one man who was in the service for thirty years. When he retired he was getting a salary of $2,000, having started at a salary of about $1,000. The man who succeeded him started off where he left off, but the man who has retired must try to live on $29, $39, or whatever he is getting.
We know the cost of living has gone up 100 per cent, and in fact this man is really getting only $14 a month as a retirement allowance. Surely with these large surpluses, surely with the desire to hide this surplus so that it will not look too large to the hungry people, there is an opportunity to look after these people who have retired from the railway, from the postal service or other departments of government.
A great many people have been harping on this question during the last four years. Surely this class is not going to be left unprotected. Many of these people have had to use what little savings they had in order to live, and some of them have had to sell their properties. It is most unjust that no consideration is being given to them. I appeal to the Minister of Finance and the cabinet around him to give consideration to these people who have been forced to retire on these small allowances.
There is every reason for granting them an increase. Civil servants still in the service have received three or four increases, which they deserved, because the cost of living has gone up. But these people have no power behind them and they cannot get anything. If they were still employed at low wages they could go out on strike. But the government considers they have not much influence and therefore they will do nothing for them.
I appeal to the minister that he use some of this huge surplus for this purpose. Surely these people should be given enough to live on without having to go to the poorhouse or ask for assistance from the community chests.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words about these large sums of money which the taxpayer is being compelled to pay. This is not all due to increases in superannuation; much of it is due to the fact that members of parliament, or at least a large number of them, are always calling for some sop to the public. This government continues to pass out these sops which in my opinion are absolutely unnecessary on many occasions in order to mollycoddle the public more than they have been mollycoddled ever before in the history of Canada. The result is that they have to increase the number of civil servants.
The result is that the taxpayer is going to be called upon to pay all these different items and the poor old pensioners cannot get a liveable allowance from this government. As the previous speaker said, they cannot go on strike and they get nothing. It is pretty nearly time that this government, supported by the opposition, put its foot down and said, "No more expansion of the civil service in order to give the Canadian people a lot of things they are not entitled to." They get all these things and then they will not pay for them without growling. We should stop this.
Like every member, I get these notices all the time advertising positions of $3,000, $4,000, $5,000, $6,000, $7,000. They are all new appointments. They represent an expansion in the civil service. I am all for giving the men who are doing a necessary job in running the affairs of this country a liveable wage, I am all for giving the retired pensioner an increase, but I am against this government continuing to employ people in order to satisfy the whims of hon. members, myself included. I would be glad to hear about this when the government denies me some things I am not entitled to.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock the minister and I were discussing this matter and I do not intend to pursue it at any length just now. But I would like to remind him of some figures in connection with this problem which I think underline its urgency. I was glad to hear the hon. member for Queens stress the need of something being done for this class of people right away.
An answer to a set of questions which I had asked is reported on page 583 of Hansard of March 19. It indicates that there are 371 retired civil servants receiving pensions of less than $20 per month.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Those are probably the ones with very short service.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is the same answer the minister gave last time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has no less validity.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is still less than $20 per month.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They might well have other sources of income.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: But it is still too little to live on if that is all they have. There are 1,616 whose pensions are less than $40 per month. Similarly there are 877 widows of retired civil servants whose pensions are less than $20 per month, and 2,527 widows whose pensions are less than $40 per month. As the hon. member for Queens has said, this matter has been raised a dozen times or more in the last few years and I hope that when the minister is giving consideration to this whole problem, as indicated by the announcement that the Civil Service Superannuation Act is to be amended, he will not overlook the plight of these civil servants who are already retired.

I believe hon. members who have thus far discussed this particular matter have done the job very well, and I merely wish to associate myself with them in the stand they have taken. First of all, I want to say that we should not necessarily retire people at the age of 65 years. I believe the time of retirement should depend upon a man's physical fitness and his ability to do the job.
I certainly resent the fact that so many of our superannuated civil servants have such low incomes. It is a shabby way in which to deal with those who have spent their lives, or a large part of their lives, in the service of the state. I want the minister to know that when the time comes to revise the act he will have the support of the Social Credit group if he wants to be more generous to civil servants who are retired.

There is a question I should like to ask the minister along the lines of my earlier inquiries. I will discuss only item 586 because apparently that will be the recurring item. It was the same figure last year; it is $75 million this year, and it may be more next year, but I imagine it will be in the order of $75 million until actuarially-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If I may interrupt my learned friend, the statement I made this afternoon was that as it was reasonable to do so, we would reduce the deficit. I am speaking from memory, but after this $75 million is applied it will be something in the order of $212 million. In addition to that, we will keep the fund strictly current from now on. It may be $25 million next year or it may be $50 million.
Supply-Finance
I am referring only to that portion which is to be appropriated from time to time to make up for the previous actuarial deficit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Right.

I should like to ask the minister whether the amount for this year, $75 million, is an amount which he and his advisers take into consideration as being an item in the estimates and to be included in the total expenditures for the year, or rather the anticipated expenditures for next year, for which he has to budget and which is accordingly reflected when he strikes his tax rate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, I think that some provision should be made for it. Speaking personally now, as Minister of Finance, I think that substantial amounts such as $75 million applied in reduction of an actuarial deficit should be made when revenues are relatively buoyant, as was the case this year when revenues have been appreciably higher than we had expected. I do not think it would be reasonable to expect that we should impose additional taxes in order to fill this hole too rapidly, if I may so describe it. That would represent my attitude, but I do not know what attitude some other minister of finance might have. It seems to me that is a fair and reasonable way in which to approach it.
As I indicated, we propose to credit the account with interest on the full amount of the actuarial liabilities so that we will, in effect, be crediting the superannuation account with interest on the $212 million which will not yet have been paid in.

I am not trying to start a discussion as to how much we should budget for each year for this purpose. I am interested in finding that whatever amount is to be paid in is included in the actual sums for which the minister budgets, and on the basis of which the tax rates are set. That is what I think should be questioned because, as the minister has said, this is a book entry. It is a transfer from the budgetary surplus into the civil service superannuation fund, but no cash goes in there.
Now, I am unable to understand-I do not want to prolong this discussion for it may be simply that I do not understand accounting, but I shall make the observation now, and when there is not the pressure of time, I shall follow it up-I am unable to understand why we should tax ourselves to raise the money when apparently no cash transfer is involved. It seems to me we are taxing ourselves to raise the same money twice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I appreciate my hon. friend's co-operation in saying that we can discuss it

Supply-Finance
in more detail later, perhaps when the superannuation act is before us. Before we do that, I would suggest to him that perhaps he might find it helpful if he were to examine the explanation in the earlier part of the public accounts of just this sort of thing, the difference between budgetary and cash charges. There is quite a good elaboration in there under the heading of the superannuation account.

There is one thing which the minister said which I should like explained. He spoke about keeping the accounts strictly current from now on. On page 6, the report the minister tabled says that there is no provision in these rates for future increases in the general level of salaries. Is that consistent with what the minister said about keeping it strictly current?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think so. I am not an actuary, of course, but I am told that the present rate of 6 per cent for men, with a matching contribution by the government and a contribution by the government for past services if the civil servant is entitled to pay in his share and claim that, will keep the account current, provided each time there is an increase in salary the government puts in a contribution which will bring it in line. That is what the $23 million is here to cover, the actuarial liability for the increase in salaries which we granted last December.

Miscellaneous grants-
5S7. Contribution towards the national women's organization program in connection with the prosecution of a thrift campaign, not to exceed $10,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The National Council of
Women and the Canadian Association of Consumers last year put on a campaign to encourage thrift. I must say that in view of the increase in savings, whether it is due to the campaign the ladies put on, it has been most successful. In the last nine months the rate of savings in Canada has nearly doubled. Whatever may have been the reason, I am sure the ladies' campaign contributed to it. They approached me, through the Bank of Canada I may say, and

asked whether the government would be prepared to make some contribution to assist in the printing of a booklet, the travelling expenses which some of them had, and so on. I took it up with my colleagues and we agreed that we should pay up to $10,000 which was appropriated out of the vote for unforeseen contingencies.
In order that the house may have an opportunity of asking me about it, I put an item in here to reimburse that account.

I had a letter the other day from a church in my riding asking for a page in a cookbook which was to cost $15. I am going to advise them to apply to the Bank of Canada, because they are pikers asking $15 for a whole page. Here we are growling about taxes and we have to pay $10,000 to tell people how to save.

1 am inclined to agree with the member who has just spoken. I think those expenditures are in the category of luxury spending. I feel that grants of this kind should be cut out in the coming year. It is one way in which we could cut down. After all, I suppose there will be a $5 billion budget, and the minister is always asking about ways in which we can cut his expenditures. Here is one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I wish that I could get some suggestions for savings in really substantial amounts. I have high admiration for the work that is done by the National Council of Women and the Canadian Association of Consumers. They are very representative organizations of women. We make grants to many worthy things. When the executive of this organization came to me, it seemed a reasonable thing to assist this worth-while work to that extent. If all the grants were as well spent as that, I would not be too worried.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Could the minister say
whether there have been contributions to either of these organizations in the past, and could he say whether it is intended to repeat this contribution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, this is once and for all. The ladies decided that here was a great chance to help fight inflation by encouraging saving. They asked the government for $10,000 to assist them in their travelling expenses and so on. So far as I am aware, it is one of those non-recurring things.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is it not the case that there was a grant of about $15,000-I am just speaking from memory-to the Canadian Association of Consumers three or four years ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There has been an annual grant to the Canadian Association of Consumers, but that is for their regular, annual operation and has nothing to do with the program to encourage saving. It wets to encourage efficient ways of consuming, and so on.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What is the amount of that annual grant?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is in the estimates. I have not got it here. I think it is either $10,000 or $12,000.
I take it from what has been said that there is nothing else contributed to the national women's association during 1951?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: 1 would not say that from memory. All I can tell the hon. member is that this is a special contribution to this special campaign put on by these two women's organizations. I would have to look at the estimates. I think we make a grant to the Girl Guides Association and to some other things.

The general opinion of this association, and it has been borne out here tonight, is that it is doing a great advertising job for the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance says that it is a wonderful organization, and doing great work. It has been doing a great advertising job for him.
Oh no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps he needs it.

It is really good propaganda for him, and the whole government is benefiting by it. I do not say it is a straight Liberal organization, but I do say that before any moneys are voted for it it should be thoroughly investigated. We should find out how the money is being spent, where it is being spent and in whose interests it is being spent. From what has been said, there is no doubt the hon. minister looks upon it as a very good organization.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In case there is any misapprehension, I assure the committee that the National Council of Women is a strictly nonpartisan organization. I know a number of the executives, and one of them was quite actively working against me in one election. I do not hold that against her. She is a very fine woman.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I do not ask that time be taken tonight-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told it is $6,000 for the vote for the Canadian Association of Consumers.

DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR General administration-
592.	To provide for the effective organization and use of agricultural manpower, including recruiting, transporting and placing workers on farms and related industries and assistance to the provinces pursuant to agreements that may be entered into by the Minister of Labour with the provinces and approved by the governor in council-further amount required, $50,000.

I want an explanation of that item. With respect to this $50,000 item I read from page 19 giving the particulars the following:
To provide for expenditures to be borne by the federal government for the effective organization and use of manpower in agriculture and related industries and assistance to the provinces pursuant to agreements entered into, including undischarged commitments of previous years.
May we have an explanation of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. I shall be happy to give it. The explanation is as follows. Harvesting operations in western Canada last year were delayed because of adverse weather conditions and in October when harvesting became general a tight farm labour situation existed in the prairie provinces.
To supplement the farm labour force in the prairie provinces, the federal government, at the request of the prairie provinces, authorized the granting of special leave to members of the armed forces who volunteered for harvest work in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.
The arrangement was that servicemen who were granted special leave for harvest work were supplied with transportation from their units to place of employment and return transportation on the expiration of the leave period. Approximately 2,000 servicemen were granted leave for this purpose.
Perhaps I do not need to go into a long and detailed explanation as to how that amount was made up; but that is the main portion of this $50,000. There is a provision in our farm labour agreements with the provinces for sharing of expenses incurred in connection with the movement of farm workers and the cost of carrying out this special movement of servicemen. This particular vote which provides for that type of expenditure in general was not sufficient to cover that extra movement.

To provide for expenses that may be incurred in the arranging for and the movement of workers from outside Canada to work on farms and other essential industry in Canada when Canadian labour is not available to meet the need; including costs connected with the supervision and welfare of persons already immigrated to Canada under former authorized labour movements and administrative expenses connected therewith-further amount required, $457,895.
Can we have an explanation of this item-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
-as to how it compares with the items under the immigration branch?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is an additional vote of $457,000. Part of it covers salaries and wages as a result of the increase. The biggest single item, $285,000, covers foods and other supplies. The item as a whole is required in order to meet commitments for reclassifications and salary increases authorized during the year; to provide funds to cover the general salary revision authorized with effect from December 1, 1951; and to offset overtime compensation for casual employees at the hostels which occurred as a result of the large influx of immigrants necessitated by the winding up of the international refugee organization activities. As I say, the largest single item of the total supplementary vote was $285,900 for food and other supplies in connection with the immigration problem to which I have just referred.
These are immigrants coming into this country from foreign countries abroad?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I believe that is the case; yes.

I wonder if the minister could say whether any money is provided there for educational purposes. Some of the municipalities have been put to considerable expense in providing classes in order to teach these immigrants English. I was wondering whether any provision was made for that purpose. Urgent requests have been made for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: From the detail which I have, I would say not; but it may be possible that there is something available under some general heading. The specific detail does not indicate that any portion of this vote is for that purpose.

I think this matter is something which is unfair to our own unemployed people. I say that because last fall several men asked me whether they could get transportation from Prince Edward Island to Ontario in order to work on a farm up there. While they had a job in sight they did not have the means of getting there. They applied to get some assistance from this vote, and they were notified that if they were aliens or were newcomers that had just come in, they would get free transportation and would be taken care of with regard to all expenses while getting to Toronto. But men from our own province were not allowed one nickel. They had to go to work and finally sacrifice some little of their belongings, with the proceeds of which they hired a car and went through to Ontario where the three of them are very

well located on two quite large farms up there. I want to say this to the minister. Why is this provision not made so that our young men wanting to move from one province to another can have the same terms as are available to those who come into our country from Europe? I think that our sons and daughters who might want to transfer from one province to another should not be discriminated against, for lack of means, in getting jobs in some other province.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend will look up vote 194 in the current estimates and the similar vote in last year's estimates he will see that there is a provision for that movement of farm workers between different parts of Canada in accordance with agreements entered into with the provinces.
Only in certain seasons.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

Where is this going to stop? We are spending the taxpayers' money. We have heard here tonight that we are paying for a portion or all of a man's fare and his food and to whom we have said "Come to Canada" in order to give him a chance to settle. Then we hear that we should pay for Canadians who can talk our language and who have had the advantage of an education costing approximately $5,000. It is said that we should tote them back and forth from one end of this country to the other and1 feed them. I for one am absolutely against that sort of thing. Any fellow who was born in this country, or any woman, can hitchhike to where they know there is work. If they cannot do that, the sooner they walk into the river until their hat floats, the better.

speechtext:
May I remind the minister of an item that appeared in the press a few days ago, the authenticity of which I have checked. I should like to express my view to the Minister of Finance about it. Suppose, for Instance, that any of us, on doctor's orders or for any other reason decided to go somewhere for a vacation at Easter, our travelling expenses were allowed.

speechtext: I would hope so.
Give him a one-way ticket.
Would that be classed as a pressure group?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I think it should be said in all fairness that this request was made by only one member of the other place. There is nothing in the Senate Hansard to indicate whether anybody else agreed with him. But I would think the minister would recognize the views of this house as expressed by the comments that have been interjected while I have been speaking, and that it would be
926	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare pretty clear that we would think that the situation should stand as it is, and that the hon. gentleman's request should not be met.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would assume that no one in this house would press that point.

In the past I have never taken what might be called a crack at the Senate, and I do not intend to start now, but I should like an explanation as to why that house with 102 members should require $5,500 of this item for travelling expenses, while this house of 262 members requires $8,000. They travel more slowly.

speechtext: In other words, it would not be along the lines of the request I referred to. We can be assured that they do not get their expenses anywhere else than to their homes.

DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE National health branch-
Health services-
606. Immigration medical services-further amount required, $508,250.

May I ask a question here, because I am getting a little bit confused. This is immigration. We have had an item under citizenship and another one under labour, and now we have one under national health and welfare. There is also one under external affairs. I suppose if there was a supplementary estimate for national defence, we would find one there. Can the minister please explain what these medical services
[Mr. Knowles.l

are for these immigrants, and whether there is a medical service set up in the Department of Citizenship and Immigration as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
We have no
medical services of our own. All of o<ur medical services are provided by the Department of National Health and Welfare. The additional grants here I am quite sure are due to the fact that last year we required more doctors abroad. We had greater facilities such as X-ray machines and the like in order to handle the larger number of immigrants who came.

Do you mean to say that the Department of National Health and Welfare administers medical services abroad to assist the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, the Department of Labour and the Department of External Affairs? Do you also have representatives of the Minister of National Health and Welfare in circulation over there?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: They had to examine a number of intending immigrants. That is what I meant when I said they did our medical services for us.

If you look at the details you will find an amount of $65,000 for travelling expenses of the staff, and allowances, $62,533. That seems to be a terrific amount, and I was wondering whether the minister could explain how that was arrived at.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can explain that. The sum of $65,000 is mainly the travelling cost of nineteen additional doctors sent to Europe. It is their travelling expenses while performing their duties there.

I think we want something a little more definite on item 606. The minister, when he was answering, said he felt quite sure that this was the case, but I want to know more definitely. Are we to take it that medical services are working for the Department of Citizenship and Immigration and for the Department of Labour, both of whom I understand do carry on operations abroad? Are we to understand that there are officers there reporting direct to the Department of National Health and Welfare, and is that a sensible organization?

I was not in the house when this matter came up. The general practice of the government is to try to centralize in one department the medical services of the government in so far as it is possible, and we now service the Department of Citizenship and Immigration just as we do other departments of the government other than veterans affairs. Our services are naturally predicated upon the policy of the government in respect

of immigration. That policy has been stated here as an accelerated one, and it requires more doctors and more equipment, and consequent expenses based upon the policy of the day on immigration.
Here we have $508,000. Now, that did not all happen overnight.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The sum of $117,000 of that is for salaries and wages. The sum of $62,000 is moneys for expenses such as nineteen additional doctors. The sum of $235,000 is for medical and other professional and special services, because in some cases the departmental doctors are not in the locality, and professional services have to be engaged for the examination of intending immigrants, particularly in view of the enforced program of X-raying of all immigrants who come to the country. A sum of $65,000 is for travelling expenses, estimated, and the sum of $800 for postage, and an estimated sum of $1,000 for telephones and telegrams.
Does this also include the expenses at Hong Kong in connection with the Chinese immigrants coming to this country?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Not with respect to any of these particular supplementary items.
Can the minister give us more detail of the examination that is carried out by these doctors over there before immigrants are accepted? Are X-rays taken of the immigrant?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: As I said, X-rays are taken of every immigrant, and when the immigrant himself is not X-rayed he has to provide the plates taken by his doctor in places where there are no departmental doctors available.
Is X-ray equipment sent over there today with these doctors, or is X-ray equipment over there made available to us?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Some X-ray equipment has been sent over. It has been found cheaper to purchase the X-ray equipment in most instances there.

I understand it is quite possible for an immigrant coming to this country, if there is no X-ray equipment at the port of exit, or where he is coming from, to go to hospital and get an X-ray plate and then take it to the immigration officer. I also understand that it is not always the X-ray plate of the immigrant that is shown.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Well, it may happen.

I understand that it is not always the X-ray plate of the immigrant that is produced.
Supply-Health and Welfare

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: My hon. friend made the statement, and I just nodded that perhaps that does happen in some instances.
Is anything being done to stop that sort of thing?
Well, of course every precaution is taken. My hon. friend may be sure of that.

Did I understand from what the Minister of Finance said when he gave us the figure of nineteen doctors that the item for medical and other professional and special services of $235,000 is for these nineteen doctors?

speechtext: No.

With respect to the item for medical and other professional and special services, as I said, it is not possible always to use the departmental doctors. speechtext: 610. Transportation; movement of mail by land, air and water, including administration, further amount required, $1,614,000.

I note that this is divided into an amount of $914,000 for mail service by railway, $300,000 for mail service by ordinary land conveyance, including rural mail delivery, and $400,000 for mail service by air. This, I understand, is an additional expenditure over the year ending December 31, 1951. If the Postmaster General were in his seat I would have a proposal to make to him with reference to couriers both on the railway lines and the rural mail couriers. In 1947 a promise was made by the then postmaster general, and it was renewed by the one who followed him, that a committee of the House of Commons would be set up to study the problem of rural mail couriers. However, no action has been taken on that.
The postmaster general who has just left office did not even show us the courtesy of looking into it, or making an explanation of it. Even in the absence of the Postmaster General, I would point out that the contracts of rural mail couriers are still far from what they should be, both from the standpoint of their being inadequate to maintain a decent standard of living, and for other reasons.
Further consideration should be given in connection with the renewal of those contracts. What did the department do in my constituency only the other day? There had been employed a man who had given faithful service over a good many years. Someone had found out that it was possible that, occasionally, he had cast a vote for the right party-the Conservative party. That person then got busy, and went around canvassing people to put in tenders for the work this man had been doing.
Under the new act the department was not obligated, as it was formerly, to accept the lowest tender. Yet, for the sake of five dollars on a $1,500 contract, this man was let go, a man who had given service for eight or ten years, and who did not have a black mark against him.
The whole situation is ridiculous. I tell our Postmaster General that we expect something more from him than the mere promise of a committee to investigate the contracts of rural mail couriers. We know there is tremendous discrimination in them. I pointed out

at the last session instances in my own constituency where the condition was most unfair. One man was driving seventeen miles, another was driving twenty-seven and another eighteen. The man who was driving eighteen miles was receiving $1,000 more than the man who was driving twenty-seven. The discrimination is so great that it should be given attention. It is all figured out, in most cases, on a political basis. I want to have this on the record so that the Postmaster General, who is not in his seat tonight, as he should be, may take notice of what I have said, and give us a fair break when the contracts are renewed.

When the main estimates for the year ending 1951-52 were brought down there was an increase of $6,789,614 over the amount which had been estimated for the previous year. Then with great fanfare and trumpeting we were told during the debate on the estimates, and the debates which followed, that a general improvement was to be introduced to the service, that a lot of economies were to be made, and that the walks for the various mail couriers were to be changed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That has nothing to do with this item, as my hon. friend appreciates.
It is going to. I am just explaining.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The carriage of mail gets heavier and heavier all the time, and the costs are related to the volume of mail carried.

Then there is $300,000 for an upward adjustment of the contract rate, where the annual cost is $1,000 or less-that is the rural mail courier to which my hon. friend was referring. Then there is $400,000 as an additional amount requested for mail service by air, due to the rapid increase in the volume of mail transported by transatlantic air mail service. There has been a tremendous increase in the volume of mail on the transatlantic air mail service, and a corresponding increase in the revenue, I may say. speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Last year or the year before we passed the Department of Transport Stores Act providing for the erasing of certain stores that were destroyed by fire or became obsolescent. The largest part of that amount of $125,000 is for the loss of articles in the department at the Moncton fire.
What about insurance?
How does this work out?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The government carries its own insurance.

How does this work out? If we vote money for the purpose of buying stores, and that is now taken care of by the Department of Transport Stores Act, why, when we lose stores, should we vote more money? Are we not voting money twice over for the same purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: This is provided by virtue of the act. If my hon. friend looks at section 8 of the act he will see there that the Minister of Transport, with the approval of the treasury board, may direct the deletion from stores inventory of obsolete or unserviceable stores or stores lost or destroyed. That is being done under the authority of that act.
Was an investigation made into this fire in Moncton and was any report made to the government of the loss of those stores?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: An investigation was made into the cause of the fire. I do not recollect now what the report was but I have here a detailed statement of the amount of goods that were lost.
Was any blame attached to any person or persons?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I would have to draw exclusively on my memory it I were to answer that question, and I should not like to do so in so far as the report of the fire is concerned.
The minister used a certain phrase, in answer to a question about insurance. He said "We carry our own insurance." Will the minister be a little more specific about that matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. The character of government assets is such that we have a sufficient distribution of risks to make it more economical for the government to carry its own insurance, or to carry its own risk, rather than to pay premiums on government property. We have a sufficiently wide area over which to distribute the possibility of loss as well as or better than any private insurance company, so it is a standard practice for governments not to pay over premiums to insurance companies. It is more economical to insure ourselves.

I think I understand that. But their practice is actually followed. Do you in fact charge to revenue each year a certain amount for insurance? As a matter of fact, it is another way of saying that we do not have any insurance at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course. The government is its own insurer.

Oh, no; it
is not as simple as all that. There are people who do what the minister said a moment ago that we do and which I know we do not do. There are people who do actually carry their own insurance and make it a real affair. As I understand it, the minister says that we follow a different plan. I am not saying for the moment whether it is right or wrong, but it is not carrying insurance. It means that we do not carry any insurance, as I understand it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are arguing about terminology. We are our own insurer.
Sometimes the government carries insurance. Is that not so? Do they not carry insurance on their steamships?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not answer that question offhand. There may be some special cases.

I will answer the question for the minister. I will give him examples showing that they do carry insurance occasionally. The S.S. Charlottetown was lost
Supply-Transport
some years ago when she was on her way up to Saint John to be repaired. She was insured the day before she pulled up anchor to leave Borden. She was insured for $1 million and that insurance was paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: That was insurance against fire.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was not referring to marine insurance. I was referring to fire insurance on buildings and equipment.
It would have been the same with fire insurance.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: No.
Suppose she had taken fire up in the yards at Saint John, New Brunswick. It would have been all the same thing.

Certain of the comments we make appear to be the cause of merriment, but that is quite all right. I should like to understand why it is that the item reads as follows:
To provide for reimbursement of the Department of Transport stores account . . .
rather than to authorize the writing off of the stores? As I understand the situation, the bulk of this item is made up on account of stores that have been burned. Why is it to be to reimburse the account for which we have already voted money rather than to authorize the writing off of stores to the value of those which were destroyed?

speechtext:
I thought I had explained that matter to my hon. friend a moment ago by referring to the section. I read part of it but I did not read the whole of it. I thought it was sufficient to read the part I read, but let me read the whole of it. It is chapter 34 of the statutes of 1950, amending the Department of Transport Stores Act. Section 8 of the act reads as follows:
The Minister of Transport, with the approval of the treasury board, may direct the deletion from stores inventory of obsolete or unserviceable stores, or stores lost or destroyed, and the value of stores so deleted shall be credited to the stores account and charged to appropriations that may be made by parliament for this purpose from time to time.
That is the reason it is set out in that fashion.
